name: Quercetin
lead: Quercetin is a plant flavonol in the polyphenol group of flavonoids. It occurs in many fruits, vegetables, leaves, seeds and grains, with capers, red onions and kale among the foods containing appreciable amounts, and it is used as an ingredient in dietary supplements, beverages and foods.[1] The name has been used since 1857 and derives from the Latin for oak forest, after the genus Quercus.[1] Average dietary intake is estimated at 25 to 50 mg per day.[1]

In longevity research quercetin is best known as the "Q" in dasatinib plus quercetin (D+Q), the first widely studied senolytic combination, which aims to remove senescent cells.[2][3] Small early-phase human trials of D+Q have been run in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, diabetic kidney disease, Alzheimer's disease and bone loss after menopause, but those studies use quercetin together with a cancer drug and cannot show what quercetin alone does.[4][5][6][7] Supplements are also marketed for inflammation, allergy and general health, and Wikipedia states that there is no high-quality evidence that quercetin in supplements or food treats cancer or any other disease.[1]

Oral absorption is poor. One reference account concludes that bioavailability is likely below 1 percent and cautions that effects seen in vitro are unlikely to carry over to the body because of rapid metabolism.[1] No clinical study of quercetin for skin, hair or facial appearance was identified.

paras: Quercetin is the aglycone (sugar-free) form of a family of flavonoid glycosides, including rutin and quercitrin, found in citrus, buckwheat and onions.[1] It is the backbone of other flavonoids such as rutin and hesperidin, as one T Nation poster notes.[8] Plants make it from phenylalanine through the phenylpropanoid pathway, with naringenin and dihydroquercetin as intermediates.[1] Red onions have higher concentrations in the outer rings, and quercetin is present in various honeys.[1] Grokipedia lists further dietary sources including apples, berries, broccoli, green tea and red wine.[9]

After oral intake quercetin is rapidly conjugated, mainly by glucuronidation, to metabolites such as quercetin-3-glucuronide, 3'-methylquercetin-3-glucuronide and quercetin-3'-sulfate. The glucuronides have a half-life of about 11 to 12 hours, whereas intravenous quercetin shows a terminal half-life of roughly 2.4 hours.[1] Aglycone supplements are less bioavailable than the glycosides in foods such as red onion, and fat or carbohydrate in a meal may increase absorption.[1] A 2025 systematic review of 31 human intervention studies examined how formulations and food matrices change bioavailability, and reported, for example, that quercetin-3-O-oligoglucosides had about twofold higher bioavailability.[10] Reviews of dietary quercetin and kaempferol describe the link between bioavailability and cardiovascular-related activity.[11] Chemists have synthesised derivatives to address its low solubility and poor bioavailability.[12]

Laboratory and animal studies report anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antiviral and anti-carcinogenic effects, and effects on platelet aggregation and capillary permeability.[13][14] Quercetin is an old tool compound in kinase research: a classic 1994 paper described it as inhibiting phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, which led to the development of the inhibitor LY294002,[15] and later work found it affects many protein kinases.[16] It binds estrogen receptor beta in competition assays, and phytoestrogen activity of this sort is the basis for caution about hormonal effects.[17][1] As a senolytic, quercetin is hypothesised to act on pro-survival pathways in senescent cells, in combination with dasatinib.[3][18]

Quercetin is sold over the counter as a supplement, typically marketed for antioxidant support, immune and allergy support, cardiovascular health and healthy ageing.[1][19] Reviews describe candidate uses in age-related diseases,[19] viral infection,[20] and as a template for drug design.[12] A traditional Chinese medicine meta-analysis for chronic atrophic gastritis also includes quercetin in its network pharmacology analysis.[21] Combination homeopathic products listing quercetin exist on the US market with the standard statement that homeopathic claims have not been reviewed by the FDA.[22]

Senolytic combination trials. A first-in-human open-label pilot in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis gave D+Q to patients,[4] followed by a 2023 phase I single-blind randomised placebo-controlled pilot of feasibility and tolerability.[5] A preliminary report from a trial in diabetic kidney disease examined whether D+Q reduced senescent cells in humans.[23] A phase 1 feasibility trial in mild Alzheimer's disease was published in Nature Medicine in 2023,[6] and a 2024 phase 2 randomised trial examined intermittent senolytic therapy and bone metabolism in postmenopausal women.[7] These trials were designed mainly to assess feasibility, tolerability and biomarkers, and they combine quercetin with dasatinib, a prescription cancer drug.

Quercetin alone. A 2019 review of quercetin in inflammation and immunity notes that much of the evidence is in vitro or in animals,[13] and Wikipedia says oral quercetin in human subjects has not shown the effects seen in laboratory models.[1] Registered studies include quercetin for COVID-19 prophylaxis and treatment (n=447),[24] GERD and oesophageal barrier function,[25] COPD,[26] post-caesarean pain,[27] metabolic health in ageing (terminated, n=5),[28] coronary disease in postmenopausal women,[29] hepatitis C,[30] and rare disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita and XIAP deficiency.[31][32] A trial of D+Q for accelerated ageing in mental disorders is ongoing.[33] A randomised trial of apple consumption examined short-term biomarkers,[34] and a trial of lotus leaf extract in overweight patients tested a mixed extract, not isolated quercetin.[35]

A 2022 meta-analysis of micronutrients found moderate- to high-quality evidence of lowered cardiovascular risk factors for several supplements, including quercetin, though that review covered all supplements and not quercetin in isolation.[36] No clinical study has tested quercetin for appearance outcomes such as skin quality.

Wikipedia reports that little research has examined the safety of quercetin supplementation in humans, that data on pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents are lacking, and that animal findings raise questions about oestrogen-dependent tumours.[1] Quercetin can interfere with some medications, with the nature of the interaction known for some drugs but not many.[1] A T Nation poster notes that chronic high doses of flavonoids such as quercetin have been reported to lower serum iodine.[37] The FDA acknowledged high-purity quercetin as generally recognised as safe in certain foods in 2010 at up to 500 mg per serving, and has also sent warning letters to manufacturers claiming that quercetin products treat diseases, which it regards as unauthorised health claims.[1]

Quercetin is part of the standard supplement shelf in bodybuilding and longevity forums. On T Nation, members mention taking it alongside resveratrol, fish oil, vitamin D and metformin while on testosterone replacement therapy,[38] list it among flavonoids in diets,[39] or recount recommendations to use it with ginkgo and green tea extract for long-COVID fatigue.[40] Others cite its presence in grape skins alongside catechins and resveratrol in rodent fitness studies.[41] Another poster points to phytoestrogens such as quercetin and genistein as dietary compounds that have not been shown to change testosterone levels in adults.[42] No looksmax.org or Reddit material was identified.

timeline.event: The name quercetin is first used, derived from the Latin quercetum, oak forest.[1]
Quercetin is reported as a PI3-kinase inhibitor, leading to the inhibitor LY294002.[15]
Aging Cell paper on the vulnerabilities of senescent cells introduces dasatinib plus quercetin as senolytics.[18]
Mouse study reports that senolytics improve physical function and increase lifespan in old age.[3]
First-in-human pilots of dasatinib plus quercetin in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease.[4][23]
FDA acknowledges high-purity quercetin as GRAS for certain food categories.[1]
Phase 1 Alzheimer's feasibility trial and phase 2 postmenopausal bone trial of senolytic therapy published.[6][7]

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums quercetin is treated as a background supplement for inflammation, immunity and general health, and more recently as a senolytic ingredient.[38][40]

claims.claim: Quercetin is a senolytic that clears senescent cells
claims.believers: Longevity enthusiasts cite the dasatinib plus quercetin research as showing that senescent cells can be removed to improve healthspan.[3]
claims.experts: The trials to date are small early-phase studies of the combination with dasatinib; quercetin alone has not been shown to clear senescent cells in published human trials.[4][5][6]

claims.claim: Quercetin helps with COVID and long-COVID fatigue
claims.believers: T Nation posters recommend quercetin with ginkgo and green tea extract for fatigue after COVID, citing flavonoid research.[40]
claims.experts: A registered trial of quercetin for COVID-19 prophylaxis and treatment enrolled 447 people,[24] and a review describes quercetin's antiviral potential mainly from laboratory studies.[20]

claims.claim: Quercetin is an anti-inflammatory antioxidant that protects health
claims.believers: Forum members include it in daily stacks and cite its role as a flavonoid backbone with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties.[8][38]
claims.experts: In vitro and animal models show anti-inflammatory activity, but Wikipedia says oral quercetin has not produced the desired effects in humans and no high-quality evidence supports disease treatment.[13][1]

claims.claim: Quercetin affects hormones or iodine status
claims.believers: One poster says chronic high doses of flavonoids such as quercetin can lower iodine serum levels, while another says dietary phytoestrogens like quercetin do not change testosterone in adults.[37][42]
claims.experts: Quercetin binds estrogen receptor beta in assays, and Wikipedia notes animal hormonal effects raise questions about oestrogen-dependent tumours; human safety data are limited.[17][1]

claims.claim: Quercetin improves skin, anti-aging or appearance
claims.believers: Supplement marketing and longevity discussion link senolytic and antioxidant effects to healthier-looking ageing.[19]
claims.experts: No published human trial has tested quercetin for appearance outcomes; reviews of benefits focus on age-related diseases in preclinical settings.[19]
